title: SSH keys, tokens & the GitHub CLI
objectives: Tell an HTTPS remote from an SSH remote by its URL, say what each authenticates with, and switch a clone with `git remote set-url`
Create an Ed25519 key with a passphrase, let the agent and Keychain hold it, and give GitHub only the `.pub` half
Read `ssh -T` and `ssh -G` output (exit 1 is success) and order `~/.ssh/config` so a second account's `Host` alias offers the right key
Choose a fine-grained token, `gh auth login` or `GH_TOKEN` for a person vs a script, and explain why logins and passphrases belong in your own terminal
Run the clone → branch → PR → review loop with `gh repo clone`, `gh pr create`, `gh pr checkout` and `gh pr view`

questions.prompt: `git remote -v` shows `origin  git@github.com:acme/api.git`. When you push, what proves who you are?

options.text: An SSH key pair on your machine, matched against a public key on your GitHub account
A personal access token from the macOS Keychain
Your GitHub password
The token `gh auth login` stored, whichever protocol the remote uses

questions.explanation: `git@github.com:owner/repo.git` is an SSH URL, so authentication is the key pair. An `https://github.com/…` URL would use a token, usually supplied by a credential helper (the Keychain helper, Git Credential Manager or `gh`). Your account password works for neither — GitHub removed password authentication for git operations. Switch protocols per clone with `git remote set-url`.

questions.prompt: GitHub's "New SSH key" form wants a key. What do you paste?

options.text: The contents of `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub`
The contents of `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`
Both files, so GitHub can verify the pair
Only the `SHA256:…` fingerprint `ssh-keygen` printed

questions.explanation: The `.pub` file is the public half: safe to share, and it's what GitHub matches your connection against. The file without `.pub` is the private key; it never leaves your machine, and pasting it anywhere means generating a new pair. The fingerprint is a short hash for *recognising* a key, not the key itself.

questions.prompt: `ssh -T git@github.com` prints `Hi ada! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access.` and `echo $?` prints `1`. Is SSH set up correctly?

options.text: Yes — exit 1 is expected here; the username in the greeting is the real result
No — any non-zero exit means the connection failed
No — GitHub refused the shell because the key lacks permissions
Only for reading; pushing needs exit code 0

questions.explanation: `-T` asks for no terminal, GitHub authenticates you and then declines to run a shell, so the command exits 1 — GitHub's docs say to expect exactly that. What to check is the **name**: it's the account the key belongs to. A real failure looks different: `Permission denied (publickey).` with exit 255, which is `ssh` itself failing.

questions.prompt: Your `~/.ssh/config` starts with `Host *` → `IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519` (personal), then `Host github-work` → `HostName github.com`, `IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_work`, `IdentitiesOnly yes`. Pushing to `git@github-work:acme/api.git` fails with `ERROR: Permission to acme/api.git denied to ada-personal.` Why?

options.text: Both identity files apply, in file order, so the personal key is offered first; GitHub accepts it and you're signed in as the personal account
`Host *` comes first, so it overrides everything below it and the work block is ignored
The work account lacks write access to `acme/api`
`github-work` isn't a real host, so ssh connected somewhere else

questions.explanation: In `ssh_config` the first value obtained wins, and every matching `IdentityFile` is added to the list in file order — `ssh -G github-work` shows the personal key listed first. GitHub accepts the first key it recognises and identifies you by it, so authentication *succeeds* as the wrong account. The work block isn't ignored (its `HostName` still applies); it just comes too late. Put specific `Host` blocks first and defaults last, or keep `IdentityFile` out of `Host *`.

questions.prompt: A small script will add labels to issues in `acme/api`, and nothing else. What credential should it use?

options.text: A fine-grained token limited to `acme/api`, with Issues read and write, and an expiry
A classic token with the `repo` scope, so it never hits a permission error
Your SSH key, since it already works for pushes
Run `gh auth login` inside the script each time it starts

questions.explanation: GitHub recommends fine-grained tokens: one owner, optionally specific repos, and per-area permissions — so a leaked token can label issues in one repo and do nothing else. A classic `repo` token reaches every repository your account can. SSH keys authenticate git, not GitHub's API, which is what labelling uses. `gh auth login` is interactive; a script gets its token from the environment (`GH_TOKEN`).

questions.prompt: A CI job needs to run `gh pr comment`. How should it authenticate?

options.text: Set `GH_TOKEN` from the CI secret store; `gh` uses it without any login
Run `gh auth login` in the job and pipe the answers to its prompts
Commit a token in a config file the job reads
Copy your laptop's Keychain entry into the job

questions.explanation: `gh` checks `GH_TOKEN` (then `GITHUB_TOKEN`) before any stored login, and its manual favours `GH_TOKEN` for fine-grained tokens — the headless path it was built for. `gh auth login` is an interactive, browser-based flow meant for a person at a terminal. A committed token is readable by everyone with repo access and lives on in git history.

questions.prompt: A teammate's PR #42 comes from their fork. You want to run it locally. Quickest correct move?

options.text: `gh pr checkout 42` — it fetches the PR's branch, even from a fork, and switches to a local branch named after it
`git switch 42`
`git pull origin 42`
`gh repo clone` the fork into a second folder and copy the changed files across

questions.explanation: A PR number is a GitHub concept; `git` has no branch called `42`, and `origin` doesn't contain a fork's branches. `gh pr checkout` resolves the number through the API, fetches the head branch from wherever it lives, and gives you a local branch (named after the PR's head branch unless you pass `--branch`). Copying files between clones loses the history you're reviewing.

prompts.prompt: Generate the key type GitHub's instructions use, with your email as the comment.
prompts.explanation: `-t ed25519` picks the key type; `-C` sets the comment at the end of the public key (without it, OpenSSH writes `user@hostname`). Run it in your own terminal so you can type a passphrase.

prompts.prompt: On macOS, load the key into the agent automatically and keep its passphrase in the Keychain.
prompts.explanation: `AddKeysToAgent yes` adds the key to the running agent the first time it's used; `UseKeychain yes` (Apple's OpenSSH) looks the passphrase up in the Keychain. `ssh-add --apple-use-keychain` asks for the passphrase once and stores it there (before macOS 12 the flag was `-K`). The private key itself never leaves `~/.ssh`.

prompts.prompt: Point an existing HTTPS clone at the SSH URL instead.
prompts.explanation: The protocol lives only in the remote's URL. `git remote set-url` swaps it; branches, history and upstream settings are untouched. `git remote -v` confirms it.

prompts.prompt: Give a second account its own alias that connects to GitHub and offers only the work key.
prompts.explanation: `HostName` maps the made-up alias to the real host; the alias only selects this block. `IdentitiesOnly yes` stops `ssh` from also offering whatever keys the agent holds. Put this block **above** any `Host *` defaults: the first value obtained wins. Clone with `git@github-work:acme/api.git`.

prompts.prompt: Open a draft PR from your branch using the commit messages, then check out a teammate's PR #42.
prompts.explanation: `gh pr create` (alias `new`) opens the PR, offering to push the branch first if it isn't pushed; `--fill` takes the title and body from your commits, `--draft` marks it not ready for review. `gh pr checkout` (alias `co`) fetches a PR's branch — fork or not — and switches to it.

snippets.question: Which `user` does ssh resolve, and which key file is listed first?
acceptable: ada, and the personal key first
snippets.explanation: `ssh_config` keeps the **first** value it obtains for each setting, reading matching blocks top to bottom. `Host *` matches everything and comes first, so `User ada` wins over `User git`. `IdentityFile` accumulates instead of being replaced, in file order — so the personal key is offered before the work key. Swap the blocks and `-G` prints `user git` with the work key first.

code: # run from a script: no terminal attached
Enter passphrase for "./ci_key" (empty for no passphrase): Enter same passphrase again:
% ssh-keygen -y -P "" -f ./ci_key > /dev/null && echo "opens with an empty passphrase"
snippets.question: What do the last two commands print?
snippets.answer: 0, then: opens with an empty passphrase
acceptable: 0 and the key has no passphrase
snippets.explanation: With no terminal to read from, ssh-keygen read the passphrase from standard input, which was empty — an empty answer, twice. It exited 0 and wrote a key with **no** passphrase, and nothing in the output says so. Make keys you'll use yourself in your own terminal; if an automation key really must be unencrypted, write `-N ""` so it's visibly deliberate. (Checked with OpenSSH 10.2 on macOS.)
